title: Scope, site classification and authority
audience: Pool and spa technicians, cleaners and supervisors who attend pool or spa sites in any state or territory
learningOutcomes: Classify a pool or spa site as residential, spa, public, hydrotherapy or commercial before starting work
Identify the named responsible operator and confirm who holds water-treatment decisions
Compare a work order with the site and state in writing which tasks are inside and outside scope
Stop and refer work when a listed trigger is present

instruction.heading: Why classification comes first
instruction.body: Pools and spas are not one hazard class. A private backyard pool, a hotel spa, a public aquatic centre and a hydrotherapy pool in a health facility each have different users, different responsible people and different duties. Before you touch a skimmer, a pump or a dosing line, establish which type of water you are working on, who operates it and what your work order allows. The classification decides who may test water, who may adjust chemistry, which records are kept and who must be told about a problem. Do not classify a site from the customer's description alone. Check the signage, the equipment, the operator's details and the venue type.

instruction.heading: Who holds responsibility
instruction.body: The operator may be the owner, a body corporate, a facility manager or a contracted pool operator. A contractor engaged for surface cleaning or equipment servicing is not automatically the operator. Before work starts, confirm the named responsible person, their contact details and whether they have delegated any treatment, closure or reopening decisions in writing. If nobody is named, treat the site as having no authorised operator and do not start treatment work.

instruction.heading: Reading the work order against the site
instruction.body: The signed work order is your scope. Check whether it covers cleaning, equipment servicing, chemical dosing, testing or inspection only. Anything beyond the written order needs a new written instruction from the responsible person or a referral to a specialist. A completed cleaning task never, by itself, makes a pool ready for use. Record the task you were engaged for and the tasks you were not engaged for, so that the record cannot later be read as a water-quality approval. If the work order includes a visual look at the safety barrier, record it as a visual check under “Safety barrier visual check and escalation”. A visual check is not a barrier approval.

instruction.heading: Operator plans and rules that vary by state and territory
instruction.body: Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan. The plan sets which products are used, the target ranges, the testing frequency, the closure triggers and the records to be kept. Where the plan is not available, stop treatment work and ask the responsible person for it. This course gives no target values. Barrier rules, registration and public-pool rules come from each state and territory and from local councils, so they vary across Australia. A rule quoted from one jurisdiction applies to that jurisdiction only. In Western Australia, the Health (Aquatic Facilities) Regulations 2007 cover aquatic facilities open to the public, and the Department of Health page (last reviewed 12 December 2023) says domestic pools are left out. In NSW, a pool's entry on the Swimming Pool Register is not a finding of compliance, as the NSW owner page (last updated 16 March 2026) explains.

instruction.heading: Stop and refer triggers
instruction.body: Stop and refer when any of these applies: there is no named responsible operator; you are asked to override a regulatory or operator-plan requirement; the task needs a licence or competence you do not hold, such as electrical, gas or confined-space work; the water shows signs of contamination; a barrier defect leaves the water reachable; or you are asked to certify the pool as safe, compliant or open. A refusal is a correct decision when the trigger is present. Record it with the time, the person asking and the reason.

procedure: Read the signed work order and write down the tasks it covers.
Classify the site type: residential, spa, public, hydrotherapy, commercial or other.
Identify the named responsible operator and record their contact details.
Obtain the site operating plan or the operator's written instruction for any water-treatment task.
Confirm the state or territory for the site and the barrier authority listed in “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”, if a barrier is in question.
Mark each planned task as inside scope, operator-only, or specialist-only.
Record the classification and scope decision before touching equipment.
Stop and refer if any stop-work trigger is present.
Record the outcome, the person informed and the time.

workedExamples.situation: A contractor is booked for a surface clean at a public aquatic centre. The duty officer says: just check the chlorine and top it up so the pool can reopen this afternoon.
workedExamples.reasoning: Water treatment and the reopening decision belong to the operator under the site plan. The contractor is engaged for surface cleaning only. The contractor declines the dosing and the reopening decision, asks for the operator's written instruction, records the request, the time, the person and the decision, and tells the supervisor. If there is an immediate hazard, the contractor follows the site emergency procedure.

workedExamples.situation: A homeowner says the spa is theirs and asks you to empty and refill it. The spa heater's maintenance label names a different service company.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you classify and scope the job?
workedExamples.reasoning: A spa at a private home is a residential or spa site, but the heater is serviced by another company. The contractor confirms the owner's authority in writing, notes the heater's servicer, excludes heater work from scope, and checks whether draining is permitted under the local discharge rules before any water is moved (see “Water conservation and environmental release”).

equipmentAndPpe: Site operating plan or operator's written instruction
Contact sheet for the responsible person
“Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check” barrier authority table, where a barrier is in question
Basic PPE for the planned task, as set by {{business:safety.required_ppe}}

commonErrors.error: Treating a pool as residential because the owner says so.
commonErrors.prevention: Classify from the site: signage, equipment, venue type and the named operator.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a cleaning job includes water treatment.
commonErrors.prevention: The written work order defines scope. Anything else needs written instruction.
Obtain written confirmation from the responsible operator and refer the decision.

commonErrors.error: Recording the pool as safe after a cleaning task.
commonErrors.prevention: Record only the tasks completed. Cleaning is not a water-quality or reopening approval.

commonErrors.error: Assuming one state's barrier or registration rule applies across Australia.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the authority and status for the job's state or territory in “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”, and refer any point you cannot check.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Water treatment compliance depends on the local operator plan. Where the plan sets treatment, testing, closure or record requirements, those requirements govern the work. This lesson sets no target value.

Safe Work Australia advises storing incompatible chemicals well apart, because mixing them can give off gases that are poisonous, flammable or damaging to materials. Never store or mix pool chemicals with acids or other incompatible goods. See “Disinfection chemistry and pH interpretation” and “Dosing systems and chlorine-gas prevention”. Refer to the product label, the SDS and the operator for storage and separation.
This lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to operate regulated pool plant or to treat water for a public or commercial pool.
Pool barrier, registration and public-pool rules are set by each state, territory and council. See “Pool-barrier rules by state and territory: where to check”.
The WA example in this lesson (Health (Aquatic Facilities) Regulations 2007) applies in Western Australia only. The Department of Health page says it covers aquatic facilities open to the public.

qualityStandard: States the site classification, the named responsible operator and the scope limit in writing before starting
Declines any task outside the written scope and records the referral
Does not record a site as safe, compliant or ready for use on the basis of cleaning work
Names the state or territory and records any barrier-related point as unresolved where it has not been established.
documentationEvidence: Site classification and the basis for it
Name and contact of the responsible operator
Scope decision: tasks in, out, and referred
Time, person contacted and decision for any referral or refusal
summary: Classify the pool or spa before work; the site type sets the users, the responsibilities and the records.
The operator holds water-treatment decisions. A cleaning contractor does not reopen a pool.
The work order is the scope. Record what is out of scope as well as what is in it.
Water treatment depends on the operator plan. Barrier and registration rules differ by state and territory.

knowledgeChecks.question: A contractor is engaged for surface cleaning at a commercial pool. There is no named operator and the duty officer asks the contractor to adjust the chlorine. What is the correct first response?
options: Adjust the chlorine to the usual range and record the change in the pool log book today
Decline water treatment, record the request, and ask for the named operator's written instruction
Ask a swimmer on site to decide what should happen with the chlorine and the pool today
Drain part of the pool to reset the chemistry, since that is quicker than adjusting it on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must the site type be established before work starts?
options: It only affects the invoice that the business sends out to the client
It sets the users, responsibilities, permitted tasks and records for the water
Residential and public pools are handled identically once the owner signs
It is needed only if the pool is larger than a set size in square metres

knowledgeChecks.question: A cleaning checklist is complete for a commercial pool. What does that completed checklist show?
options: The water is safe to swim in, since the cleaning has been completed on the day and the pool is clean
Only that the listed cleaning tasks were completed; it does not show water quality or reopening approval
The operator has approved reopening of the pool to swimmers today after the clean and the check
Chemical levels are within target for the whole pool and the water at every point tested today
